baseline_rows.pred_answer: The Regulation applies a risk-based framework of four tiers plus a parallel regime for general-purpose AI models: prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems classified under Article 6 either as a safety component of, or as itself, a product covered by the Annex I Union harmonisation legislation and required to undergo third-party conformity assessment or as an Annex III use case, limited risk carrying the Article 50 transparency obligations, and minimal risk with no mandatory obligations, while general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with stricter duties where the model is classified as posing systemic risk under Article 51.

Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).

Yes, both apply where the patient-monitoring system is a high-risk AI system. The provider must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature and risks of the system, actively and systematically collecting and analysing performance data over its lifetime to evaluate continuous compliance, on the basis of a post-market monitoring plan (Article 72). Because the device is covered by the Union medical device legislation listed in Annex I Section A, Article 72(4) lets the provider integrate those elements into the post-market surveillance system and plan already established under that legislation. The provider must also report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities, immediately after establishing a causal link and no later than 15 days, 2 days for a widespread infringement or serious critical-infrastructure disruption, and 10 days on a person's death, and then investigate and take corrective action (Article 73); for a system that is itself, or a safety component of, a device under the Union medical device and in vitro diagnostic legislation, Article 73(10) limits the AI Act notification to serious incidents consisting of an infringement of fundamental rights and directs it to the national competent authority designated for that purpose, with death or serious deterioration of health routing through the vigilance system of that medical device legislation instead.

Not high-risk. An AI image generator is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which is the route to high-risk under Article 6(1), and generating images is not one of the use cases that Article 6(2) makes high-risk through Annex III. It is limited risk, and as a provider of a system generating synthetic image content it must ensure under Article 50(2) that the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, unless the system performs only an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input. It would become high-risk only where a particular deployment brings it within an Annex III use case or makes it a safety component of an Annex I product requiring third-party conformity assessment.

The high-risk radiology system must technically allow the automatic recording of events over its lifetime, with logging appropriate to the intended purpose that captures situations liable to present a risk or a substantial modification, supports post-market monitoring, and enables monitoring of the operation, as required by Article 12. As deployer, the hospital must keep the logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent they are under its control, for a period appropriate to the intended purpose and in any event at least six months, unless a longer or different period follows from applicable Union or national law, in particular data protection law, under Article 26(6).

Not determined by the compute figure standing alone, and not by the text of the Regulation. The one-third-of-base-training-compute test, under which a party that fine-tunes an existing general-purpose AI model is treated as the provider of the modified model, comes from the Commission's General-Purpose AI Guidelines of 18 July 2025, which are Commission guidance rather than text of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. That guidance treats the fine-tuner as a new provider where its training compute exceeds one-third of the base model's compute, so a fine-tune resting exactly at the threshold rather than above it does not by itself cross that line. The adopted Regulation sets no numeric fine-tuning threshold for provider status, so provider status turns on the Regulation's own operator definitions rather than on the guidance figure.

Under Article 13, the provider must design the high-risk system so its operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret its output and use it appropriately, and must accompany it with instructions for use giving the provider's identity, the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations including its intended purpose and its level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, the human oversight measures, and the computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime and necessary maintenance. Under Article 50 the provider carries two further duties, both owed to the natural persons concerned rather than to the deployer. Article 50(1) requires the provider to design a system intended to interact directly with natural persons so that they are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious, with a carve-out for systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Article 50(2) requires the provider of a system generating synthetic audio, image, video or text to mark the outputs in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, except where the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data.

Under Article 23(1), before placing the high-risk AI system on the market the importer must verify four matters. It must verify that the provider has carried out the relevant conformity assessment procedure, that the provider has drawn up the technical documentation, that the system bears the required CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and instructions for use, and that a provider established in a third country has appointed an authorised representative in the Union in accordance with Article 22(1). Where the importer has sufficient reason to consider the system non-conforming, falsified, or accompanied by falsified documentation, Article 23(2) bars it from placing the system on the market until brought into conformity, and where the system presents a risk it must inform the provider, the authorised representative and the market surveillance authorities.

A fundamental rights impact assessment, which Article 27(1) requires a deployer that is a body governed by public law to perform before first use of a high-risk system evaluating eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services under Annex III(5). That assessment must describe the deployer's processes in which the system will be used, the period and frequency of its intended use, the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them taking account of the information the provider gives under Article 13, the human oversight measures according to the instructions for use, and the measures to take if those risks materialise, including internal governance arrangements and complaint mechanisms. Once the assessment is performed, the deployer must notify the market surveillance authority of its results using the template developed by the AI Office (Article 27).

Yes, but only the provider-side one. Under Article 50(2) the provider of the generative AI system must ensure the synthetic text output is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. The marketing team acts as deployer, and the deployer text-disclosure duty in Article 50(4) is confined to text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, which promotional copy is not, so it is not triggered here. No deployer transparency obligation attaches to publishing the promotional copy.

This question is about the Product Liability Directive (PLD), not the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This assistant only covers EU AI Act questions; consult the Product Liability Directive (PLD) for the applicable rules.

Minimal-risk AI systems are the residual category: systems that are neither prohibited under Article 5, nor high-risk under Article 6 (as an Annex I safety component or an Annex III use case), nor subject to the Article 50 transparency duties, nor general-purpose AI models. Typical examples are AI-enabled spam filters, inventory-management tools, and AI in video games. They carry no mandatory obligations under the Regulation, though providers and deployers may adopt voluntary codes of conduct.

No. Inferring the emotions of natural persons in the workplace is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(f), and monitoring manufacturing line workers' emotions to improve efficiency falls squarely within that prohibition. The only carve-out is where the emotion recognition system is put into service or placed on the market for medical or safety reasons, and improving efficiency is neither, so the practice is not permitted. Monitoring physical states such as fatigue for accident prevention would sit within the safety carve-out, but emotion and stress monitoring for productivity does not.

A deployer of a high-risk AI system must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), ensure input data it controls is relevant and sufficiently representative (Article 26(4)), monitor operation and, where the use may present a risk, inform the provider and the market surveillance authority and suspend use, reporting any serious incident (Article 26(5)), keep the automatically generated logs for at least six months (Article 26(6)), inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use (Article 26(7)), comply with the registration obligations where it is a public authority (Article 26(8)), inform natural persons subject to Annex III decisions (Article 26(11)), and cooperate with the competent authorities (Article 26(12)). Where the deployer is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of the Annex III(5)(b) or (c) systems, it must also perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use and notify the market surveillance authority of the results (Article 27). Where a decision taken on the basis of an Annex III system's output produces legal or similarly significant adverse effects, the deployer must give the affected person a clear and meaningful explanation of the system's role in the decision (Article 86). The provider-only design and conformity requirements do not bind the deployer unless it becomes a provider under Article 25 by putting its name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or changing its intended purpose.

High-risk. An AI system used for the recruitment or selection of natural persons, including to place targeted job advertisements, to analyse and filter job applications, and to evaluate candidates, is a listed use case under Annex III(4)(a), which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk. The classification is displaced only where the system falls within the Article 6(3) derogation, meaning it performs a narrow procedural, result-improving, pattern-detection or preparatory task and poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, though a system that performs profiling of natural persons remains high-risk in all cases.

Not high-risk. A system that only transcribes doctor-patient consultations and performs no diagnosis or decision-making does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, and it is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which are the only two routes to high-risk classification under Article 6(1) and Article 6(2). It is therefore explicitly not high-risk and does not carry the Chapter III high-risk obligations. Should the tool's function be extended to materially influence clinical decisions, the classification would need to be reassessed against Article 6.

Prohibited. Monitoring call centre agents' stress levels is inferring emotions of natural persons in a workplace, which Article 5(1)(f) prohibits, and selling the system for that purpose is itself placing it on the market for a prohibited use. The medical or safety carve-out in Article 5(1)(f) does not reach ordinary performance or stress monitoring of staff, so it would apply only if the system were genuinely intended for a medical or safety purpose such as fatigue detection to prevent accidents.

Under Article 72, the provider of a high-risk AI system must establish and document a post-market monitoring system proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the system (Article 72(1)). That system must actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant performance data throughout the system's lifetime, drawn from deployers and other sources, so the provider can evaluate the system's continuous compliance with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements (Article 72(2)). The monitoring must rest on a post-market monitoring plan that forms part of the technical documentation set out in Annex IV (Article 72(3)). Under Article 73, the provider must report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where it occurred (Article 73(1)), immediately after establishing a causal link and in any event within 15 days of becoming aware (Article 73(2)), within two days for a widespread infringement or a serious incident consisting of a critical-infrastructure disruption (Article 73(3)), and within 10 days where a person has died (Article 73(4)). Following the report the provider must, without delay, perform the necessary investigations, carry out a risk assessment, take corrective action, and cooperate with the competent authorities without altering the system in a way that could affect the evaluation of the incident's causes before informing them (Article 73(6)).

Yes, the risk level changes fundamentally, because the engagement-scoring feature is emotion recognition applied in the workplace, which Article 5(1)(f) lists as a prohibited practice rather than merely a high-risk or limited risk one. Reading employees' facial expressions to infer their engagement is inferring emotions of natural persons in the area of the workplace, and the only carve-out is where the system is put in place for medical or safety reasons, which scoring engagement is not. The meeting-notes summarisation on its own remains limited risk, carrying only the Article 50 transparency duty to inform staff they are interacting with an AI system, but bolting on the facial-expression engagement score moves that feature into the prohibited tier and it cannot lawfully be deployed on staff.

Not high-risk. An email spam filter that sorts incoming messages into junk and inbox does not fall within any of the eight Annex III use cases, and it is not a safety component of, or itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, so neither route of Article 6 classifies it as high-risk. It is not among the prohibited practices either. It therefore sits in the minimal risk tier and carries none of the high-risk provider or deployer obligations, subject only to any general transparency duty that would arise if the system were later designed to interact directly with natural persons or to generate synthetic content.

Excludes military/defence/national-security uses, scientific R&D, purely personal non-professional use, and free/open-source AI systems outside the high-risk + prohibited + transparency scope. Classifies an AI system as high-risk on two routes. Annex I route (Article 6(1)): the system is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I AND that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that sectoral legislation. Annex III route (Article 6(2)): the system falls within one of the eight Annex III use cases. Article 6(3) derogation: an Annex III system is NOT high-risk where it poses no significant risk of harm and meets one of four conditions (a narrow procedural task; improving the result of a previously completed human activity; detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment; or a preparatory task), unless it profiles natural persons, in which case it is always high-risk; the provider must document this self-assessment before placing the system on the market and still register it under Article 49(2). Where the high-risk system is an Annex-III biometric-identification, emotion-recognition, or biometric-categorisation system, Article 26(11) preserves the Article 50 transparency-to-end-user obligations on top of the Article 13 transparency-to-deployer chain.

No. Article 13 and Article 86 impose different duties on different actors for the benefit of different people. Article 13 is a provider duty of transparency and provision of information to deployers, requiring high-risk AI systems to be designed for sufficient operational transparency and to be accompanied by instructions for use so the deployer can interpret the output and use it appropriately. Article 86 is a right to explanation of individual decision-making owed by the deployer to an affected person, who, where a decision taken on the basis of the output of an Annex III high-risk system (other than the Annex III(2) critical infrastructure systems) produces legal effects or similarly significantly and adversely affects their health, safety or fundamental rights, may obtain clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision.

No. Inferring the emotions of natural persons in the workplace is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(f), and monitoring manufacturing line workers' emotions to improve efficiency falls squarely within that prohibition. The only carve-out is where the emotion recognition system is put into service or placed on the market for medical or safety reasons, and improving efficiency is neither, so the practice is not permitted. Monitoring physical states such as fatigue for accident prevention would sit within the safety carve-out, but emotion and stress monitoring for productivity does not.

‘systemic risk’ means a risk that is specific to the high-impact capabilities of general-purpose AI models, having a significant impact on the Union market due to their reach, or due to actual or reasonably foreseeable negative effects on public health, safety, public security, fundamental rights, or the society as a whole, that can be propagated at scale across the value chain;

The purpose of the Regulation, stated in Article 1, is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems, and supporting innovation.

Not regulated as a prohibited or high-risk practice. An AI opponent in a video game is not among the exhaustively listed prohibited practices in Article 5, and it does not fall within any Annex III use case, so it is not high-risk under Article 6(2); nor is a video game a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, so the Article 6(1) route does not apply either.

Before placing a high-risk medical diagnostic system on the market, the provider must ensure it satisfies all the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and bears the provider's identifying details, as required by the overarching provider duty in Article 16. The system must meet the substantive design requirements of Article 8, supported by a documented, iterative risk-management system running across its lifecycle under Article 9, and data-governance practices ensuring the training, validation and test datasets are relevant, representative, complete and examined for bias under Article 10. The provider must draw up the technical documentation before placing the system on the market, demonstrating conformity and containing the content specified in Annex IV, as required by Article 11.

The Digital Omnibus falls outside the version applied here, which is Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as adopted, so its deferred dates, revised categories and renumbered articles are not applied. Under the adopted text the high-risk AI system obligations apply from 2 August 2026, and from 2 August 2027 for the Annex I safety-component route, and those dates govern the answer.

Under Article 9, the provider must establish, implement, document and maintain a risk management system, run as a continuous iterative process throughout the high-risk AI system's lifecycle, that identifies and analyses the known and reasonably foreseeable risks to health, safety or fundamental rights, estimates the risks arising in intended use and under reasonably foreseeable misuse, evaluates risks from post-market monitoring data, and adopts appropriate and targeted risk management measures, with the system tested against prior-defined metrics to select those measures. Under Article 10, where the high-risk AI system is trained with data, the provider must develop it on training, validation and testing data sets that are relevant, sufficiently representative, to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose, and subject those data sets to data governance and management practices covering design choices, data collection processes and the origin of data, data preparation such as annotation, labelling, cleaning and aggregation, formulation of assumptions, assessment of availability and suitability, examination for possible biases, measures to detect, prevent and mitigate those biases, and identification of relevant data gaps. Article 9 further requires the provider to consider whether the system is likely to have an adverse impact on persons under 18 or other vulnerable groups, and Article 10 permits the exceptional processing of special categories of personal data strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, subject to the safeguards it sets out.

No high-risk crossing. Auto-suggesting canned replies is not one of the Annex III high-risk use cases and the system is not a safety component of a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation, so it stays outside the high-risk tier. It can, however, engage the limited risk transparency layer: under Article 50(2) a provider whose AI system generates synthetic text must ensure the output is marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, an obligation that does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input. Separately, where the system is designed to interact directly with natural persons, Article 50(1) requires those persons to be informed that they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person.

Prohibited under Article 5(1)(g), which bans biometric categorisation systems that categorise natural persons individually on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation. Inferring race, political opinions and sexual orientation from facial images falls squarely within that provision.

Article 73 governs the reporting of serious incidents, requiring providers of high-risk AI systems placed on the Union market to report any serious incident to the market surveillance authorities of the Member States where that incident occurred (Article 73(1)).

Distributor obligations for a CE-marked high-risk biometric system are set by Article 24. Before making it available on the market, the distributor must verify that it bears the CE marking and is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use, and that the provider and importer have met their labelling obligations (Article 24(1)). Where the distributor considers the system is not in conformity with the Section 2 requirements it must not make it available until it is brought into conformity, and where the system presents a risk it must inform the provider or importer (Article 24(2)), and once the system is on the market it must take or ensure corrective action to bring it into conformity, withdraw or recall it, informing the competent authorities where it presents a risk (Article 24(4)). The distributor must also keep storage and transport conditions from jeopardising compliance (Article 24(3)), provide competent authorities on reasoned request with the information and documentation demonstrating conformity (Article 24(5)), and cooperate with those authorities in any action to reduce the risk the system poses (Article 24(6)).

The seven guiding principles of the EU AI Act are articulated in Recital 27 (the trustworthy-AI framework) and inform the human-centric purpose of Article 1: human agency and oversight; technical robustness and safety; privacy and data governance; transparency; diversity, non-discrimination and fairness; social and environmental wellbeing; and accountability. Article 4 operationalises these principles by requiring providers and deployers to ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among their staff.

A notified body must be involved wherever the medical device is itself required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union medical devices legislation, since that legislation, not the internal-control route, then governs. Under Article 43(3), a high-risk AI system covered by that legislation, which is listed in Section A of Annex I, follows the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedure, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that single assessment. A notified body designated under the medical devices legislation is entitled to control the AI system's conformity with those requirements, provided its compliance with the notified-body requirements has been assessed in the context of that legislation's notification procedure. Where that legislation allows the manufacturer to opt out of third-party assessment because it applied all harmonised standards, no notified body is required, and the AI medical device follows the same route only if the manufacturer has also applied the harmonised standards or common specifications covering the Section 2 requirements.
Human oversight measures for high-risk AI systems are governed by Article 14.

Not high-risk in itself, and not a prohibited practice. A general customer service chatbot falls within none of the Annex III use cases and is not a safety component of a product regulated under Annex I, so Article 6 does not classify it as high-risk; it would become high-risk only where it is deployed for one of those Annex III uses or is such a safety component requiring third-party conformity assessment. As a system intended to interact directly with natural persons, it carries the provider's transparency duty under Article 50(1) to ensure users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious in the circumstances.

High-risk where the software is itself, or is a safety component of, a medical device that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, which is what Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk. Diagnostic software that detects melanoma from dermoscopy images is a medical device, and such a device in this diagnostic function is placed in a risk class that requires notified-body involvement, so the two cumulative conditions of Article 6(1) are met and the system is high-risk. Under Article 43(3) the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required by that medical-device legislation, and the requirements of Chapter III Section 2 apply as part of that assessment. The deciding fact is whether the device requires third-party conformity assessment under the Annex I legislation.

No. Article 88(1) vests exclusive supervision and enforcement of the Chapter V obligations of general-purpose AI model providers in the Commission, which entrusts the implementation of those tasks to the AI Office, but that provision confers supervisory and enforcement powers rather than any power to levy a fine. The administrative fines are governed by Article 99, whose ceilings are laid down by the Member States, and under Article 99(9) those fines are imposed by competent national courts or other national bodies depending on the Member State's legal system. The AI Office therefore does not itself directly impose fines under Article 88.

Annex I and Annex III mark the two distinct routes by which Article 6 classifies a system as high-risk. Under the Annex I route, Article 6(1) makes a system high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Under the Annex III route, Article 6(2) makes a system high-risk where its intended use falls within one of the eight use-case categories in Annex III, namely biometrics, critical infrastructure, education and vocational training, employment and worker management, essential private and public services, law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control, and administration of justice and democratic processes. The difference is that Annex I turns on the product and its sectoral safety regime, whereas Annex III turns on the purpose of use, and only the Annex III route carries the Article 6(3) derogation under which a system posing no significant risk of harm and performing a narrow procedural, result-improving, pattern-detection or preparatory task is not high-risk, unless it profiles natural persons.

The applicable procedure is conformity assessment based on internal control, the self-assessment route Article 43 assigns to the employment use cases in Annex III, which for a recruitment and CV-sorting system does not involve a notified body. Under that route the provider itself verifies that the system meets the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and that its quality management system and technical documentation are in order, rather than obtaining a third-party examination. Conformity is then demonstrated under Article 16 by drawing up the EU declaration of conformity, affixing the CE marking, and registering the system in the EU database before it is placed on the market.

The obligation falls on the deployer under Article 50(4), which requires a deployer of an AI system that generates or manipulates image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake to disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated. Where the video forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, that duty is limited to disclosing the existence of the generated content in a manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work. The duty does not apply where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute a criminal offence.

Not high-risk, and the transparency regime largely does not bite. Translating incoming messages is not among the listed high-risk use cases, so the system falls outside the high-risk tier and its Chapter III requirements. Article 50(2) does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, which a faithful translation preserving the meaning of the original message will ordinarily satisfy, so in practice this feature is limited risk carrying at most the Article 50(1) disclosure where it is not already obvious to the user.

The SaaS company is the provider, and the enterprise customers configuring the system for their own hiring are deployers. As the entity that develops the CV-screening AI and makes it available under its own name, the SaaS company carries the provider obligations, and the recruitment and candidate-evaluation function is a high-risk use case under Annex III(4)(a). A customer would itself become a provider under Article 25(1) only where it puts its name or trademark on the system, makes a substantial modification to it, or modifies its intended purpose so that the system becomes or remains high-risk, and routine configuration for its own hiring does none of these. Absent those circumstances the customer remains a deployer, subject to the deployer obligations in Article 26.

An AI system that sorts patients by their biometric data to set priority for an experimental clinical trial is not, in itself, a listed high-risk use case, because prioritising trial participants is neither emergency healthcare patient triage nor evaluation of eligibility for essential healthcare services under Annex III, so the tier turns on what the biometric sorting does. It is prohibited where that sorting categorises individual natural persons on the basis of their biometric data to deduce or infer their race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation, which Article 5(1)(g) bars as biometric categorisation. It is instead high-risk where it performs biometric categorisation according to other sensitive or protected attributes based on the inference of those attributes, a use case listed in Annex III(1)(b) that Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk. Absent either of those biometric functions, the system is not high-risk under these classification rules.

An AI system intended to interact directly with patients is, at minimum, subject to the transparency duty in Article 50(1): the provider must design it so that patients are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless that is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. Where the chatbot generates synthetic audio, image, video or text, Article 50(2) requires the provider to mark that output in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated. A mental health chatbot rises to high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product that must undergo third-party conformity assessment under the medical device legislation in Annex I, which is the route Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk; answering general patient queries, without a diagnostic or therapeutic function bringing it within that legislation, leaves it as a limited risk system carrying the Article 50 transparency duty alone. Because a therapeutic setting is neither a workplace nor an education institution, inferring a patient's emotions is not caught by the Article 5(1)(f) prohibition, which in any event carves out use for medical reasons.

The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.

Not high-risk and not prohibited, so an AI spam filter is minimal risk. It is neither a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, nor does it fall within any of the Annex III use cases, so Article 6 does not classify it as high-risk. Where the filter interacts directly with natural persons the provider must ensure they are informed they are interacting with an AI system under Article 50(1), but content-filtering that does not interact with people carries no transparency duty.

Not automatically high-risk. An AI system is high-risk under Article 6(2) only where it falls within an Annex III use case, and selecting and recruiting eligible patients for a clinical trial is not the recruitment or selection of natural persons for employment that Annex III(4)(a) covers, nor does it match any other Annex III category on these facts. The remaining route is Article 6(1): the system is high-risk where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, such as a medical device, that must undergo third-party conformity assessment. Absent that route it is not high-risk, and whether the clinical-trial or medical-device framework outside this Regulation imposes its own requirements falls outside the scope of the EU AI Act.

The customer has that right against the deployer. Under Article 86, any affected person subject to a decision the deployer takes on the basis of the output of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, where that decision produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects the person in a way they consider to adversely impact their health, safety or fundamental rights, is entitled to obtain from the deployer clear and meaningful explanations of the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken. A loan denial produced by a creditworthiness system is such a decision, so the deployer must provide that explanation on request. This right does not apply where exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law, and it applies only to the extent the same right is not otherwise provided for under Union law.

Article 16 sets the provider's duties for a high-risk AI system: ensure the system complies with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements and indicate the provider's identity on it, operate a quality management system, keep the technical documentation, keep the automatically generated logs where under its control, have the system undergo conformity assessment before it is placed on the market, draw up the EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking, comply with the registration obligations, take the necessary corrective actions, demonstrate conformity on a national competent authority's reasoned request, and ensure the system meets the applicable accessibility requirements. Article 26 sets the deployer's duties: use the system in accordance with the instructions for use, assign human oversight to natural persons who have the necessary competence, training and authority, ensure the relevance of input data to the extent it controls that data, monitor operation and inform the provider and market surveillance authority of risks and serious incidents, keep the automatically generated logs under its control for at least six months, inform workers' representatives and affected workers before workplace use, and cooperate with the competent authorities.

The mis-triage that harmed the patient is a serious incident within the meaning of Article 3(49), which covers the death of a person or serious harm to a person's health. The Regulation requires such a serious incident to be reported to the relevant market surveillance authority and corrective action to be taken, with the deployer cooperating to that end. The incident must also be fed into the risk management system, which under Article 9 obliges the provider to evaluate the data gathered from post-market monitoring and to adopt appropriate and targeted risk management measures to address the risk it reveals, retesting the system so that it performs consistently for its intended purpose. Any parallel reporting duty under the medical devices framework falls outside the scope of this Regulation and must be assessed under that legislation.

Not high-risk, and not otherwise regulated by tier. Inventory demand forecasting and stock re-ordering is neither a prohibited practice under Article 5 nor one of the Annex III use cases that Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk, and the tool is not a safety component of, nor itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I requiring third-party conformity assessment under Article 6(1), which is the only other route to high-risk. It would become high-risk only if it were deployed as a safety component in the management and operation of critical infrastructure such as the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity within the meaning of Annex III, which ordinary warehouse stock management is not. Absent that, the system is minimal risk with no mandatory obligations, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty only where it interacts directly with natural persons.

Because cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations, the model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities and is classified as a general-purpose AI model with systemic risk under Article 51(2). On top of the baseline provider duties in Article 53, Article 55(1) then adds four obligations: performing model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools including documented adversarial testing (Article 55(1)(a)), assessing and mitigating possible systemic risks at Union level including their sources (Article 55(1)(b)), keeping track of, documenting and reporting serious incidents and possible corrective measures without undue delay to the AI Office and, as appropriate, national competent authorities (Article 55(1)(c)), and ensuring an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for both the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(d)). Until a harmonised standard is published, the provider may rely on the codes of practice under Article 56 to demonstrate compliance with these obligations.

The "Very Large Online Platform" designation and its algorithmic transparency duties arise under separate Union platform legislation, which falls outside the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 and is not interpreted here. On its EU AI Act side, transparency under Article 50 attaches to the AI system by actor and function, not to the platform's size, so a content-moderation system carries the provider duty under Article 50(1) to inform natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system only where it is intended to interact with them directly, and the provider duty under Article 50(2) to mark outputs in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated only where it generates synthetic audio, image, video or text. Where the moderation system merely classifies or removes content without either interacting directly with persons or generating synthetic content, Article 50 imposes no transparency obligation on it. The Article 50(3) and Article 50(4) deployer duties bear on emotion recognition, biometric categorisation, deepfakes and public-interest text, none of which a content-moderation function engages by default.

High-risk, conditional on the device requiring third-party conformity assessment: an AI system that is itself, or is a safety component of, a medical device covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I is high-risk under Article 6(1) where that device must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation, which a tumour-detection diagnostic ordinarily does. The conformity assessment runs through Article 43(3): the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required under the sectoral medical-device legislation, carried out with notified-body involvement where that legislation requires it, and the Chapter III Section 2 requirements form part of that same assessment, yielding a single CE marking. The medical-device regime that supplies the notified-body procedure sits outside this Regulation and is therefore not interpreted here beyond that bridging point.

Before placing the high-risk AI system on the market, the provider must draw up technical documentation and keep it up to date, demonstrating that the system complies with the requirements of Chapter III, Section 2 (Article 11). It must contain at least the elements set out in Annex IV, namely a general description of the system, a detailed description of its development, design specifications, system architecture and computational resources, data and training methodologies, the human oversight measures, the risk management system, validation and testing procedures with metrics and test logs, cybersecurity measures, the EU declaration of conformity, and the post-market monitoring system (Annex IV). Where the provider is an SME, including a start-up, it may provide those elements in the simplified form established by the Commission (Article 11).

Article 42(1) presumes such a high-risk AI system to comply with the requirement in Article 10(4) that data sets take into account the characteristics particular to the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional setting within which the system is intended to be used.

Not high-risk, unless the translation system is put to use as a safety component of a product regulated under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)), or is integrated into one of the use cases listed in Annex III such that Article 6(2) applies. General-purpose language translation is not itself a listed high-risk use case and is not among the practices prohibited under Article 5, so absent one of those two routes it is limited risk, carrying only the Article 50 transparency duties, namely informing natural persons that they are interacting with an AI system where it does so directly and marking synthetic output as artificially generated in a machine-readable format. The deciding fact is the context of deployment rather than the translation function itself.

An AI system used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance falls within Annex III point 5(c), under the 'essential private and public services' high-risk use-case category. Classification follows the Annex III route: under Article 6(2), an AI system that falls within one of the Annex III use cases is considered high-risk. The system therefore carries the full Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk AI systems.

Still high-risk. Using the system to decide who to lay off is a decision on the termination of work-related contractual relationships, which is a listed use case under Annex III(4)(b), and Article 6(2) classifies any Annex III use case as high-risk. This use falls within the same high-risk tier as the performance evaluation, so the high-risk obligations continue to apply.

Before placing a high-risk AI system on the market, the provider must complete the conformity assessment under Article 43 and then register under Article 49. Under Article 43 the route depends on the system: an Annex III point 1 biometric system, where the provider has applied harmonised standards or common specifications, may follow either the internal control procedure of Annex VI or the quality management system and technical documentation assessment with notified body involvement under Annex VII, while the Annex III systems in points 2 to 8 follow the internal control procedure of Annex VI without a notified body, and a system covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I follows that legislation's own conformity assessment procedure into which the Chapter III Section 2 requirements are integrated as a single procedure (Article 43(3)). Under Annex VI internal control, the provider verifies that its quality management system conforms to the requirements, examines the technical documentation against the Section 2 requirements, and verifies that design, development and post-market monitoring are consistent with that documentation. The provider or its authorised representative must then register both itself and the system in the EU database referred to in Article 71 before the system is placed on the market or put into service (Article 49(1)), except for the Annex III point 2 critical infrastructure systems, which are registered at national level (Article 49(5)).

Yes, the classification changes to high-risk. A system that evaluates learning outcomes within educational and vocational training institutions is a listed use case under Annex III(3)(b), which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk, and scoring final exams to decide who passes materially influences the outcome of decision making rather than performing a narrow procedural or preparatory task, so no derogation applies. The Article 50(1) duty to inform users they are interacting with an AI system continues to apply alongside the high-risk obligations.

The provider of the AI system generating the synthetic audio and text must ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, using solutions that are effective, interoperable, robust and reliable as far as technically feasible, which is the provider obligation under Article 50(2). That marking duty does not apply to the extent the system performs an assistive function for standard editing or does not substantially alter the input data or its semantics, or where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences. Because the content is published online, the separate deployer disclosure duties under Article 50(4) may also apply: audio content constituting a deep fake must be disclosed as artificially generated or manipulated, and text published to inform the public on matters of public interest must be disclosed as artificially generated, the latter not applying where the content underwent human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility for its publication.

Article 57, which requires each Member State to ensure its competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at national level, operational by 2 August 2026, providing a controlled environment that fosters innovation and facilitates the development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems for a limited time before they are placed on the market or put into service. Its objectives under Article 57(9) expressly include facilitating and accelerating access to the Union market for AI systems, in particular when provided by SMEs, including start-ups.

Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).

Neither prohibited nor a listed Annex III high-risk use case, an AI system that transcribes doctor-patient conversations is high-risk only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a medical device covered by the Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which is what Article 6(1) classifies as high-risk. A transcription function is not among the prohibited practices in Article 5 and does not fall within any of the Annex III use cases, so absent that Annex I route it is not high-risk. Where the system interacts directly with the patient, the provider carries the Article 50(1) transparency duty to ensure the natural person is informed they are interacting with an AI system. The deciding fact is whether the transcription tool forms part of a regulated medical device requiring third-party conformity assessment.

‘general-purpose AI model’ means an AI model, including where such an AI model is trained with a large amount of data using self-supervision at scale, that displays significant generality and is capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks regardless of the way the model is placed on the market and that can be integrated into a variety of downstream systems or applications, except AI models that are used for research, development or prototyping activities before they are placed on the market;

The "Very Large Online Platform" designation belongs to the Digital Services Act, which falls outside the scope of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; the EU AI Act imposes no transparency duty keyed to that status, and its transparency rules attach to a content-moderation system by function under Article 50. Where the system is designed to interact directly with natural persons, the provider must ensure those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system (Article 50(1)), and where it generates synthetic audio, image, video or text the provider must mark the output in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(2)). The deployer-side duties arise only for their triggering functions, namely informing persons exposed to an emotion recognition or biometric categorisation system (Article 50(3)) and disclosing deepfake content, together with AI-generated or manipulated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest subject to the carve-out where the content underwent human review or editorial control and a natural or legal person holds editorial responsibility (Article 50(4)). A content-moderation system that only classifies, ranks or removes content, without interacting directly with natural persons or generating synthetic content, engages none of these Article 50 duties.

Not high-risk absent a further fact, and not among the practices prohibited under Article 5. An inventory-management tool is not one of the use cases enumerated in Annex III, so the Article 6(2) route does not apply, and it becomes high-risk under Article 6(1) only where it is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I that must undergo third-party conformity assessment, which ordinary inventory management is not. Failing that route it is limited or minimal risk, carrying the Article 50 transparency duty where the system interacts directly with natural persons.

The provider of a high-risk AI sepsis-prediction model must ensure its training, validation and testing data sets are subject to data governance practices appropriate for the intended purpose, including data provenance, collection processes, data preparation, bias examination and mitigation (Article 10(2)). The data sets must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete, with appropriate statistical properties for the intended use (Article 10(3)). Where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, the provider may process special categories of personal data under strict safeguards, including pseudonymisation, access controls and deletion upon correction (Article 10(5)). The provider must also document these data governance measures in the technical documentation, including a description of the data sets, their provenance, selection, labelling and cleaning methodologies (Annex IV(2)(d)).

Rebranding an AI system under a new name or trademark makes the rebroadening entity the provider under Article 25(1)(a). That entity must then comply with all provider obligations, including ensuring the system meets the transparency requirements for AI systems interacting with natural persons (Article 50(1)) and, where applicable, marking synthetic content as artificially generated (Article 50(2)). It must also ensure a sufficient level of AI literacy among relevant staff (Article 4). If the system is high-risk, additional obligations under Articles 9 to 15 and conformity assessment under Article 43 apply.

High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed to enable effective human oversight by natural persons during use, ensuring they can understand the system’s capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret its output, decide to disregard or override it, and intervene or stop it through a ‘stop’ button or similar procedure (Article 14). For systems referred to in Annex III(1)(a), no decision may be based on the system’s identification unless verified by at least two competent natural persons, unless Union or national law deems this disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum purposes (Article 14(5)). High-risk AI systems must also achieve appropriate levels of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity throughout their lifecycle, with accuracy metrics declared in the instructions for use (Article 15(1), Article 15(3)). They must be resilient against errors, faults, inconsistencies, and attacks such as data poisoning, model evasion or adversarial examples, and include technical and organisational measures like access controls and fail-safe mechanisms (Article 15(4), Article 15(5)).

The right to an explanation for an individual decision made or supported by a high-risk AI system is not directly established under the EU AI Act. Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed for sufficient transparency to enable deployers to interpret the system’s output, and mandates that instructions for use include information to enable deployers to interpret outputs appropriately. Deployers using high-risk AI systems that make or assist in decisions about natural persons must inform those individuals of the system’s use under Article 26(11). However, the Act does not grant individuals a standalone right to a detailed explanation of a specific decision.

High-risk. An AI system used to verify travellers' identities by detecting, recognising or identifying natural persons in the context of migration, asylum or border control management falls under Annex III(7)(d), which Article 6(2) classifies as high-risk. The provider must comply with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, including a risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), logging (Article 12), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), accuracy and cybersecurity (Article 15), and a quality management system (Article 17), and must undergo conformity assessment (Article 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), and register the system in the EU database (Article 49). Deployers must inform exposed persons of the system’s operation where it performs biometric categorisation or emotion recognition (Article 50(3)).

High-risk. An AI system used to score and rank applicants for admission is intended to determine access to educational institutions, which falls under Annex III(3)(a), a use case classified as high-risk by Article 6(2). The vendor’s claim that it is “just a recommendation tool” does not alter this classification, as the system’s intended purpose determines its risk tier. The deployer, a university, must comply with Article 26 obligations, including assigning human oversight and informing affected individuals.

The Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 August 2026, as set out in Article 113(2). This general application date covers all high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, unless a specific transitional provision applies. The obligations under Chapter III, Section 2, including risk management, technical documentation, and conformity assessment, become enforceable on that date. Pre-existing high-risk systems used by public authorities benefit from a longer transition period until 2 August 2030 under Article 113(3)(d).

Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27).

Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

Not high-risk unless it is a safety component of, or itself a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation requiring third-party conformity assessment under Annex I, or falls within an Annex III use case. A music recommendation AI is not listed in Annex III and does not engage Article 5 prohibitions such as social scoring or manipulative techniques. It is therefore not high-risk under Article 6(2) and not prohibited under Article 5. Where it interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must ensure they are informed of the AI interaction under Article 50(1).

If the chatbot generates synthetic content such as text, audio, image or video, the provider must also ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated under Article 50(2). These obligations apply regardless of the system’s risk classification and are distinct from any additional requirements under Chapter III for high-risk systems. The information must be provided in a clear and distinguishable manner at the time of first interaction.

Deployment to a real client during the sandbox phase is permitted only if the testing remains within the controlled environment of the AI regulatory sandbox and under the supervision of the competent authority, as required by Article 57(5). The sandbox allows development, training, testing and validation of innovative AI systems before market placement, including testing in real-world conditions supervised therein. Any deployment must follow the specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority and comply with risk-mitigation and oversight obligations under Article 57(6). Deployment outside the sandbox framework would require compliance with the separate real-world testing regime under Article 60, including approval by the market surveillance authority and informed consent of test subjects.

A general-purpose AI model provider must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation per Annex XI (Article 53(1)(a)), supply information to downstream providers per Annex XII (Article 53(1)(b)), implement a policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)), and publish a publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)). The obligations in Article 53(1)(a) and (b) do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, except where the model is classified as having systemic risk (Article 53(2)). A provider must additionally comply with Article 55 obligations where the model is classified as systemic-risk, which occurs if it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, or is designated as such by the Commission (Article 51(1), (2)). Those additional obligations are: performing model evaluation including adversarial testing (Article 55(1)(a)), assessing and mitigating systemic risks at Union level (Article 55(1)(b)), reporting serious incidents without undue delay (Article 55(1)(c)), and ensuring adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(d)).

Yes, it is prohibited. The inference of religious beliefs or political opinions from biometric data constitutes biometric categorisation based on sensitive attributes, which is a prohibited AI practice under Article 5(1)(g). This prohibition applies regardless of the purpose or deployer, with no exceptions for advertising or private-sector use.

The provider must ensure the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure before placing it on the market, as required by Article 16(1)(f). The conformity assessment is carried out in accordance with Article 43, which specifies the applicable procedure depending on the system’s classification under Annex I or Annex III. For systems covered by Annex I legislation requiring third-party assessment, the procedure under that legislation applies, with Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of it (Article 43(3)). For systems listed in Annex III, the provider follows the internal control procedure in Annex VI, unless otherwise specified.

Yes, where the announcement is clear and distinguishable, the voice assistant satisfies the provider's transparency duty under Article 50(1). Providers must ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. The obligation applies regardless of whether the system is high-risk, and the announcement "I am a virtual assistant" qualifies as compliant information under Article 50(5). This duty does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards.

The Commission's 18 July 2025 Guidelines presume a general-purpose AI model is one when its training compute exceeds 10^23 floating-point operations, as stated in the Guidelines. This threshold is not in the Regulation itself but forms part of the Commission's interpretive guidance.

A provider (Article 3(3)) develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A deployer (Article 3(4)) uses an AI system under its authority in the course of a professional activity, so the provider bears the design and conformity duties of Article 16 while the deployer bears the use-phase duties of Article 26. Under Article 25 a deployer, distributor, importer, or other third party becomes a provider, and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market, makes a substantial modification to such a system, or modifies a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.

An AI system used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance falls within Annex III point 5(c), under the 'essential private and public services' high-risk use-case category. Classification follows the Annex III route: under Article 6(2), an AI system that falls within one of the Annex III use cases is considered high-risk. The system therefore carries the full Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk AI systems.

Prohibited. The use of AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing or being reasonably likely to cause significant harm, is prohibited under Article 5(1)(a).Similarly, the exploitation of vulnerabilities related to age, disability, or specific social or economic situation that leads to material distortion of behaviour and significant harm is prohibited under Article 5(1)(b).

High-risk where used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for public healthcare benefits. An AI system intended to be used by public authorities or on their behalf to assess eligibility for essential public assistance services, including healthcare, is classified as high-risk under Annex III(5)(a), which Article 6(2) includes in the high-risk category. The provider must comply with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, including risk management, data governance, technical documentation, and conformity assessment, before placing the system on the market.

A provider established in a third country must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate before placing a high-risk AI system on the market (Article 22). The authorised representative ensures compliance with registration and documentation obligations, acts as a contact for competent authorities, and keeps the EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation available (Article 22).

A high-risk AI system must have a documented, iterative risk management system established, implemented and maintained throughout its lifecycle (Article 9). The system must be developed using training, validation and testing data sets that are relevant, representative, free of errors and complete, with data governance practices addressing bias and data provenance (Article 10). The provider must draw up and keep up to date technical documentation demonstrating conformity with the Regulation, containing the information listed in Annex IV (Article 11).

Yes, where the deployer is a public authority, it must verify that the high-risk AI system is registered in the EU database before use, as required by Article 26(8). If the system is not registered, the deployer shall not use it and must inform the provider or distributor. This pre-deployment check is a specific obligation for public authorities deploying high-risk AI systems. No other pre-use assessment is mandated for deployers under Article 26.

Not high-risk. A word processor using AI for spelling and grammar correction is not listed in Annex III and does not qualify as a safety component of a product under Annex I, so it is not high-risk under Article 6. It is also not prohibited under Article 5. Providers of such systems must comply with the transparency obligation in Article 50(1) to inform users they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious.

Distributors of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III are bound by Article 24. Under Annex I, Union harmonisation legislation list. Article 5 prohibits eight categories of AI practice: (a) subliminal / manipulative / deceptive. Article 9 requires a documented, iterative risk-management system across the AI system's lifecycle.

Prohibited. The untargeted scraping of facial images from CCTV footage to create or expand a facial recognition database is prohibited under Article 5(1)(e). This prohibition applies regardless of the context or purpose of the system.

For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

High-risk. A medical device software that detects cancer from MRI scans is a product covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices, which is listed in Annex I, and such devices are required to undergo third-party conformity assessment, making the AI system high-risk under Article 6(1). The provider must follow the conformity assessment procedure required under that legislation, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment, as specified in Article 43(3).

Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed with sufficient operational transparency to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. The systems must be accompanied by instructions for use containing concise, complete, correct and clear information relevant to deployers, including the provider’s identity, intended purpose, performance characteristics, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, known risks, human oversight measures, and maintenance requirements. Where the high-risk system is used for biometric identification, emotion recognition or biometric categorisation under Annex III, deployers must also comply with the end-user transparency obligations in Article 50, preserved by Article 26(11). Article 50 mandates deployers to inform natural persons exposed to such systems and to disclose deepfakes or AI-generated text published for public information purposes, subject to specified exceptions.

Prohibited. The placing on the market, the putting into service, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage is prohibited under Article 5(1)(e).

Effective human oversight requires that natural persons assigned to oversight can understand the system's capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, and remain aware of automation bias. They must be able to correctly interpret the system's output and decide to disregard, override or reverse it, or intervene in its operation, as required by Article 14. The provider must design the system to enable such oversight and specify the necessary measures in the instructions for use under Article 13(3)(d). Deployers must assign oversight to competent, trained individuals with the necessary authority, in accordance with Article 26(2).

GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 are grandfathered until 2 August 2027. Providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain technical documentation per Annex XI (Article 53(1)(a)), supply downstream providers with integration and capability information per Annex XII (Article 53(1)(b)), implement a copyright policy (Article 53(1)(c)), and publish a publicly available training-data summary (Article 53(1)(d)). The technical documentation and downstream information obligations do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, except where the model is designated as systemic-risk (Article 53(2)). Systemic-risk models, defined by cumulative training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, are subject to additional obligations under Article 55.

Article 5 prohibits specific AI practices outright, such as social scoring leading to unjustified detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts (Article 5(1)(c)), emotion recognition in workplaces and educational institutions (Article 5(1)(f)), and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement except for narrowly defined objectives (Article 5(1)(h)). Article 6 classifies AI systems as high-risk through two cumulative routes: first, where the system is a safety component of, or itself a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product requires third-party conformity assessment (Article 6(1)); second, where the system falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III (Article 6(2)). A system may be prohibited under Article 5 even if it would otherwise be classified as high-risk under Article 6, and the classification under Article 6 triggers additional obligations only if the system does not fall under the prohibitions of Article 5.

Yes, the operator's legal role changes. By putting the operator's brand on the system and making a substantial modification, the operator becomes a provider under Article 25(1). As a provider, the operator must now comply with all provider obligations, including the risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), technical documentation (Article 11), logging (Article 12), transparency (Article 13), human oversight (Article 14), accuracy and cybersecurity (Article 15), quality management system (Article 17), conformity assessment (Article 43), EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), CE marking (Article 48), and registration in the EU database (Article 49).

Yes, a provider of a stand-alone high-risk AI system must register it in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service.
