As a provider, they must comply with all applicable obligations under the Regulation, including transparency requirements under Article 50. Where the system interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must ensure users are informed of the AI interaction unless it is obvious, and any synthetic content must be marked as artificially generated in a machine-readable format. These obligations apply regardless of whether the system was previously placed on the market by another entity.

High-risk AI systems must be designed and developed to enable effective human oversight by natural persons during use, ensuring they can understand the system's capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret its output, decide to disregard or override it, and intervene or stop it through a 'stop' button or similar procedure (Article 14). For systems referred to in Annex III(1)(a), no decision may be based on the system's identification unless verified by at least two competent natural persons, unless Union or national law deems this disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum purposes (Article 14(5)). High-risk AI systems must also achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, perform consistently throughout their lifecycle, have accuracy metrics declared in instructions for use, be resilient against errors and environmental inconsistencies, and be protected against data poisoning, model evasion, and other adversarial attacks (Article 15).

The deployer must inform the applicant that the decision was made by a high-risk AI system under Article 26(11), which requires deployers of Annex III systems that make decisions about natural persons to disclose the system’s use. The instructions for use, mandated by Article 13(3)(b)(vii), must include information enabling deployers to interpret the system’s output, but the Regulation does not grant individuals a standalone right to a detailed explanation of the specific decision. The obligation to provide individualised reasoning beyond disclosure of AI use is not established in the cited provisions.

High-risk. An AI system used to verify travellers' identities using biometrics at a border crossing falls under Annex III(7)(d), which classifies AI systems intended to detect, recognise or identify natural persons in the context of migration, asylum and border control management as high-risk, provided their use is permitted under relevant Union or national law. This classification is subject to Article 6(2), which establishes that AI systems listed in Annex III are high-risk. The provider must comply with the obligations for high-risk systems, including registration in the EU database under Article 49(1) and adherence to transparency requirements under Article 50.

High-risk. An AI system used by a university to score and rank applicants for admission falls under Annex III(3)(a), which classifies as high-risk AI systems intended to be used to determine access or admission to educational and vocational training institutions. The vendor’s claim that it is “just a recommendation tool” does not alter this classification, as Article 6(2) establishes high-risk status based on the intended purpose of the system, not its marketed function. The provider must therefore comply with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and the deployer must assign human oversight and inform affected persons in accordance with Article 26.

The Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 August 2026, as set out in Article 113(2). This general application date covers all high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, subject to the derogation in Article 6(3) where a system does not pose a significant risk of harm and meets one of the specified conditions. The Commission’s guidelines under Article 6(5), due by 2 February 2026, will further clarify the practical implementation of the high-risk classification. Obligations under Article 6(1) for AI systems that are safety components of products in Annex I are deferred until 2 August 2027, per Article 113(3)(c).

Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27).

Yes. Under Article 11(1), SMEs, including start-ups, may provide the technical documentation elements set out in Annex IV in a simplified manner, using a simplified form the Commission is required to establish for the needs of small and micro enterprises. Where an SME opts to use that form, the notified body performing the conformity assessment must accept it.

Not high-risk unless it is a safety component of, or itself a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment, or falls under a use case in Annex III. A music recommendation AI is not listed in Annex III and does not engage in prohibited practices under Article 5. It is therefore not high-risk under Article 6(2) and not prohibited under Article 5. Where it interacts directly with natural persons, it is subject to the transparency obligation under Article 50(1) to inform users they are interacting with an AI system.

Article 50(1) requires providers to ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons, such as a patient-facing medical chatbot, are designed so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. Article 50(2) requires providers to mark any synthetic content generated by the system as artificially generated or manipulated in a machine-readable and detectable format. These obligations apply regardless of the system’s risk classification and are distinct from any additional requirements under Chapter III for high-risk systems. The deployer must also comply with Article 50(4) if the system generates or manipulates deepfake content or AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest.

Yes, where the deployment constitutes testing in real-world conditions under a supervised sandbox plan. Article 57(5) permits AI regulatory sandboxes to include testing in real-world conditions, provided it occurs within a controlled environment and under a specific sandbox plan agreed with the competent authority. Such testing must remain supervised by the competent authority, which provides guidance and oversight to identify and mitigate risks to health, safety and fundamental rights (Article 57(6)). The provider remains liable for any damage caused during testing, and the sandbox does not exempt the system from compliance with the Regulation’s requirements before being placed on the market.

A general-purpose AI model provider must draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation per Annex XI (Article 53(1)(a)), supply information to downstream providers per Annex XII (Article 53(1)(b)), implement a policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)), and publish a publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)). The obligations in Article 53(1)(a) and (b) do not apply to models released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, except where the model is classified as having systemic risk (Article 53(2)). A provider must additionally comply with Article 55 obligations where the model is classified as systemic-risk, which occurs if it has high-impact capabilities, presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs, or is designated as such by the Commission (Article 51(1), (2)). Those additional obligations are: performing model evaluation with adversarial testing (Article 55(1)(a)), assessing and mitigating systemic risks at Union level (Article 55(1)(b)), reporting serious incidents without undue delay (Article 55(1)(c)), and ensuring adequate cybersecurity for the model and its physical infrastructure (Article 55(1)(d)).

Yes, it is prohibited. The inference of political opinions or religious beliefs from biometric data constitutes biometric categorisation based on sensitive attributes, which is prohibited under Article 5(1)(g). This prohibition applies regardless of the purpose, including ad targeting, and permits no exceptions for such uses.

The provider must ensure the high-risk AI system undergoes the relevant conformity assessment procedure before placing it on the market, as required by Article 16(1)(f). The conformity assessment is carried out in accordance with Article 43, which specifies the applicable procedure depending on the system’s classification under Article 6(1) or Article 6(2). The provider must also draw up the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix the CE marking (Article 48), and register the system in the EU database (Article 49(1)). These steps are mandatory before market placement.

Yes, where the announcement is clear and distinguishable, the voice assistant satisfies the provider's transparency duty under Article 50(1). The provider must ensure AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so that users are informed they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person. The obligation applies regardless of the system’s risk tier and must be fulfilled at the first interaction.

The Commission's 18 July 2025 Guidelines presume a model is general-purpose when its cumulative training compute exceeds 10^23 floating-point operations, which is the new threshold for triggering general-purpose AI model classification under Article 51. This guidance also presumes high-impact capabilities for systemic risk classification under Article 51(2) at 10^25 FLOPs, and treats a fine-tuned model as a new provider under Article 25 where additional training compute exceeds one-third of the base model’s compute.

A provider (Article 3(3)) develops an AI system, or has one developed, and places it on the market or puts it into service under its own name or trademark. A deployer (Article 3(4)) uses an AI system under its authority in the course of a professional activity, so the provider bears the design and conformity duties of Article 16 while the deployer bears the use-phase duties of Article 26. Under Article 25 a deployer, distributor, importer, or other third party becomes a provider, and assumes the Article 16 provider obligations, where it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market, makes a substantial modification to such a system, or modifies a system's intended purpose so that it becomes high-risk.

Under Article 2(6), the Regulation does not apply to AI systems or models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development. Article 2(8) further excludes any research, testing or development activity on AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, except testing in real-world conditions. The Act's obligations therefore attach only once the system leaves pure R&D and is placed on the market or put into service, at which point the operator's duties follow the system's risk classification.

An AI system used for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in the case of life and health insurance falls within Annex III point 5(c), under the 'essential private and public services' high-risk use-case category. Classification follows the Annex III route: under Article 6(2), an AI system that falls within one of the Annex III use cases is considered high-risk. The system therefore carries the full Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk AI systems.

Prohibited. The use of AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing significant harm, is prohibited under Article 5(1)(a). This prohibition also extends to systems exploiting vulnerabilities related to age, disability or socio-economic situation to materially distort behaviour in a manner likely to cause significant harm, as set out in Article 5(1)(b).

High-risk where used by or on behalf of public authorities to evaluate eligibility for public healthcare benefits. An AI system intended to be used by public authorities or on their behalf to assess eligibility for essential public assistance services, including healthcare, is listed in Annex III(5)(a) as a high-risk system under Article 6(2). The provider must comply with the Chapter III requirements for high-risk systems, including risk management, data governance, technical documentation and conformity assessment. The derogation in Article 6(3) does not apply if the system performs profiling of natural persons, and even where it does not, the provider must document the assessment and register the system under Article 49(2).

A provider established outside the EU must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate before placing a high-risk AI system on the market (Article 22). The authorised representative ensures the EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation are available, keeps them for 10 years, and acts as the contact point for competent authorities (Article 22).

A high-risk AI system must have a risk management system (Article 9), data governance (Article 10), and technical documentation (Article 11). The risk management system shall be a continuous iterative process that includes identifying and analysing known and foreseeable risks, estimating and evaluating risks under intended use and reasonably foreseeable misuse, and adopting appropriate risk mitigation measures. Training, validation and testing data sets must be relevant, representative, free of errors and complete, with data governance practices covering provenance, bias examination and mitigation, and, where strictly necessary, processing of special categories of personal data for bias correction. The technical documentation must be drawn up before market placement, kept up to date, and contain the information listed in Annex IV, including system description, development process, risk management, and post-market monitoring.

Yes, where the operator is a public authority deploying a high-risk AI system, the operator must verify that the system is registered in the EU database before use, as required by Article 26(8). If the system is not registered, the operator must not use it and must inform the provider or distributor. This pre-deployment check is the operator's specific obligation as a public-sector deployer. The operator must also inform affected individuals about the system’s use under Article 26(11).

Not high-risk. A word processor using AI for spelling and grammar correction is not listed in Annex III and does not qualify as a safety component of a product under Annex I, so it is not high-risk under Article 6. It is not prohibited under Article 5. Providers of such systems must comply with the transparency obligation in Article 50(1) to inform users they are interacting with an AI system, unless this is obvious.

Distributors of a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III are bound by Article 24. Under Annex I, Union harmonisation legislation list. Article 5 prohibits eight categories of AI practice: (a) subliminal / manipulative / deceptive. Article 9 requires a documented, iterative risk-management system across the AI system's lifecycle.

Prohibited. The untargeted scraping of facial images from CCTV footage to create or expand a facial recognition database is a prohibited AI practice under Article 5(1)(e). This prohibition applies regardless of the context or purpose of the system.

For high-risk AI systems the applicable penalty ceiling is set by Article 99(4): administrative fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or, for an undertaking, up to 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, for non-compliance with the obligations on providers, deployers, importers and distributors (every obligation other than the Article 5 prohibitions, which carry the higher Article 99(3) ceiling of EUR 35 000 000 or 7 %). Under Article 99(6), for SMEs and start-ups each fine is capped at the lower of the percentage or the fixed amount. Penalties must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.

High-risk only where the medical device software is a safety component of, or is itself, a product covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment. This classification follows from Article 6(1), which requires both conditions to be met. The provider must then follow the conformity assessment procedure under Article 43(3) as required by the Medical Devices Regulation, with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment.

Article 13 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed with sufficient operational transparency to enable deployers to interpret the system's output and use it appropriately. The systems must be accompanied by instructions for use containing information on the provider, intended purpose, performance, accuracy, robustness, cybersecurity, known risks, human oversight measures, and maintenance. Where the high-risk system is used for biometric identification, emotion recognition or biometric categorisation under Annex III, deployers must also comply with the end-user transparency obligations in Article 50, preserved by Article 26(11). Article 50 requires deployers to inform natural persons exposed to such systems and to disclose deepfakes or AI-generated text published for public information purposes, subject to specified exceptions.

Prohibited. The placing on the market, the putting into service, or the use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage is prohibited under Article 5(1)(e).

Effective human oversight requires that natural persons assigned to oversight can understand the system's capabilities and limitations, monitor its operation, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret its output, and decide to disregard, override or reverse its output (Article 14). The provider must design the system to enable such oversight and specify the necessary measures in the instructions for use (Article 14(3)). Deployers must assign oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)). Where the system is used for clinical decision support, these obligations apply unless a specific derogation under Article 6(3) is met.

GPAI models placed on the market before 2 August 2025 are grandfathered until 2 August 2027. Providers of general-purpose AI models must maintain technical documentation per Annex XI and make available information to downstream providers per Annex XII, unless the model is released under a free and open-source licence with publicly available parameters, in which case the obligations under Article 53(1)(a) and (b) do not apply. All GPAI providers must implement a copyright policy and publish a publicly available training-data summary under Article 53(1)(c) and (d), regardless of licence. Where the model meets the systemic-risk threshold of 10^25 FLOPs under Article 51(2), the additional obligations under Article 55 apply and the open-source carve-out under Article 53(2) no longer applies.

Article 5 prohibits specific AI practices outright, including social scoring, emotion recognition in workplaces and education, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces by law enforcement, with narrow exceptions for each. Article 6 classifies AI systems as high-risk through two cumulative routes: first, where the system is a safety component of, or itself a product covered by, Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and that product requires third-party conformity assessment; second, where the system falls within one of the use cases listed in Annex III. A system may be prohibited under Article 5 even if it would otherwise be classified as high-risk under Article 6, and the two provisions operate independently. The classification under Article 6 triggers compliance obligations, while Article 5 renders certain systems unlawful to place on the market or use.

Yes, the operator's legal role changes. By putting the operator's brand on the system and making a substantial modification, the operator becomes a provider under Article 25(1). As a provider, the operator must now fulfill all provider obligations, including conformity assessment (Article 43), technical documentation (Article 11), risk management (Article 9), and registration (Article 49).

Yes, a provider of a stand-alone high-risk AI system must register it in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service. This obligation applies to high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III, with the exception of those referred to in point 2 of Annex III. The provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database established under Article 71. This requirement is set out in Article 49(1).

Prohibited. The use of an AI system that deploys subliminal techniques, such as timed haptic buzzes during moments of user hesitation, to materially distort behaviour by impairing the ability to make an informed decision, with the effect of causing a person to take a decision they would not otherwise have taken, is prohibited under Article 5(1)(a) where it causes or is reasonably likely to cause significant harm.

No, this is not prohibited social scoring under Article 5(1)(c). The prohibition applies only where the social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the data’s origin, or treatment unjustified or disproportionate to the behaviour’s gravity, which is not the case for an internal creditworthiness score used solely for financial risk assessment. However, the system may still be high-risk under Annex III(5)(a) if used by or on behalf of a public authority for access to essential services, or otherwise falls under limited risk with transparency obligations under Article 50 where it interacts with natural persons.

As deployer, the hospital must use the system in accordance with the provider's instructions for use, which Article 13 requires the provider to supply (Article 26(1)). The hospital must assign human oversight to natural persons with the necessary competence, training and authority (Article 26(2)), monitor the system's operation on the basis of those instructions and inform the provider of serious incidents (Article 26(5)), and retain the logs the system automatically generates (Article 26(6)). Where the hospital is a body governed by public law, a private entity providing public services, or a deployer of an Annex III point 5(b) or 5(c) system, it must perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before first use (Article 27). A person subject to a deployer decision based on the system's output that produces legal effects or similarly significantly affects health, safety or fundamental rights has a right to an explanation (Article 86). These are deployer duties only: the hospital does not bear the provider's design and conformity duties unless it becomes a provider under Article 25 by putting its name or trademark on the system, making a substantial modification, or changing the intended purpose.

The criteria for assessing the risk of an AI system include the intended purpose, extent of use, nature and amount of data processed, autonomy level, potential harm or adverse impact on health, safety or fundamental rights, reversibility of outcomes, dependency on system outputs, vulnerability of affected persons, availability of redress, and the magnitude and likelihood of benefits, as set out in Article 7(2). High-risk systems are classified under Annex III based on specific use cases such as biometrics, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice. Providers must establish a continuous risk management system that identifies and analyses risks, evaluates them under intended use and foreseeable misuse, and implements mitigation measures, as required by Article 9. Training, validation and testing data must be relevant, representative, free of errors and complete, with attention to bias and data governance, in accordance with Article 10.

The EU AI Act's core regime governs AI systems, defined in Article 3(1) and brought within scope by Article 2, through the risk-based tiers (prohibited practices under Article 5, high-risk systems under Article 6, and limited-risk transparency duties under Article 50). General-purpose AI models are regulated separately under Chapter V (Articles 51 to 56), are defined in Article 3(63), and carry their own provider obligations with additional duties for models posing systemic risk. The Regulation therefore applies to both AI systems and general-purpose AI models under two parallel regimes.

Prohibited. AI systems that deploy subliminal techniques beyond a person’s consciousness or purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques, with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour by appreciably impairing the ability to make an informed decision, thereby causing or being reasonably likely to cause significant harm, are prohibited under Article 5(1)(a). This prohibition also extends to systems that exploit vulnerabilities related to age, disability, or socio-economic situation in a manner that materially distorts behaviour and causes significant harm, as set out in Article 5(1)(b).

High-risk. An AI tool recommending oncology treatment regimens is a safety component of a medical device, which is a product covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and subject to third-party conformity assessment, making it high-risk under Article 6(1). The provider must implement a risk management system (Article 9), ensure data governance (Article 10), achieve accuracy and robustness (Article 15), and provide transparency through instructions for use (Article 13). It must also undergo conformity assessment (Article 43), draw up an EU declaration of conformity (Article 47), affix CE marking (Article 48), register in the EU database (Article 49), and maintain a quality management system (Article 17).

Yes, judicial pre-authorization is required. Each use of real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement must be subject to prior authorization by a judicial or independent administrative authority, as mandated by Article 5(3). This applies even for the targeted search for missing persons under Article 5(1)(h)(i). In duly justified cases of urgency, use may commence without prior authorization, but a request must be submitted within 24 hours, and if authorization is denied, the use must stop immediately.

Article 99 sets administrative fines for breaches of the EU AI Act, with three tiers based on the nature of the infringement. Non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5 is subject to fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). Infringements of specific operator and notified body obligations, including those under Articles 16, 22 to 24, 26, 31, 33(1), (3), (4), 34, and 50, are subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 99(4)). Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities is subject to fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 99(5)), with reduced ceilings for SMEs and start-ups under Article 99(6). Article 101 empowers the Commission, acting through the AI Office established under Article 64, to impose fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, on providers of general-purpose AI models for intentional or negligent breaches of Chapter V, failure to comply with Commission requests, or supplying false information.

Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure training, validation and testing data sets are relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete, taking into account the specific geographical, contextual, behavioural or functional settings of use (Article 10(3) and (4)). They must implement data governance practices addressing data collection, origin, preparation, assumptions, bias examination and mitigation, and identification of data gaps (Article 10(2)). Where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, providers may process special categories of personal data under strict safeguards, including necessity, security, access controls, non-transfer, and timely deletion (Article 10(5)). These requirements are part of the broader obligation to ensure data governance appropriate to the system’s intended purpose (Article 10(2)).

Where the high-risk system is an Annex-III biometric-identification, emotion-recognition, or biometric-categorisation system, Article 26(11) preserves the Article 50 transparency-to-end-user obligations on top of the Article 13 transparency-to-deployer chain. Under Article 38, Coordination of notified bodies: the Commission ensures that appropriate coordination. Under Article 16, Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure the system meets the Chapter III Section 2. Under Article 25, Responsibilities along the AI value chain: any distributor, importer, deployer.

High-risk. By placing the high-risk AI system on the EU market under its own brand, the importer becomes a provider under Article 25(1)(a) and assumes all provider obligations under Chapter III Section 2. It must ensure the system underwent the conformity assessment (Article 43), bears the CE marking (Article 48), is accompanied by the EU declaration of conformity (Article 47) and instructions for use, and verify that the technical documentation was drawn up (Article 11). The importer must also indicate its name and contact address on the system or packaging (Article 23(3)) and keep copies of the conformity documents for 10 years (Article 23(5)).

Yes, where the fine-tuning constitutes a substantial modification. A third party that modifies a general-purpose AI model becomes the provider under Article 25(1)(b) if it makes a substantial modification, regardless of the compute threshold. The Commission's Guidelines of 18 July 2025 suggest that fine-tuning exceeding one-third of the base model’s training compute may amount to a substantial modification, but this is interpretive guidance, not a binding threshold in the Regulation. As the new provider, the entity assumes full obligations under Article 53, including technical documentation (Annex XI), downstream provider information (Annex XII), copyright policy, and training data summary. If the resulting model meets the systemic risk criteria under Article 51(1), such as by exceeding 10^25 FLOPs cumulative compute, the additional obligations in Article 55 also apply.

Article 5 prohibits eight AI practices outright: subliminal or manipulative techniques causing significant harm, exploitation of vulnerabilities linked to age, disability, or socio-economic situation, social scoring leading to unjustified detrimental treatment, criminal-offence risk profiling of natural persons, untargeted scraping of facial images to build facial-recognition databases, emotion recognition in the workplace or educational institutions, biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes, and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement subject to the narrow Article 5(1)(h) exceptions.

A machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.

High-risk where the AI system is a safety component of a CE-marked medical device that is subject to third-party conformity assessment under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. The system is classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) because it concerns a product listed in Annex I and requires third-party conformity assessment. The conformity assessment follows the procedure of the applicable Union harmonisation legislation, with Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment under Article 43(3).

Prohibited. Social scoring is prohibited under Article 5(1)(c), which bans AI systems that evaluate or classify natural persons over time based on their social behaviour or personal characteristics where the resulting social score leads to either or both of detrimental or unfavourable treatment in unrelated social contexts or treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the behaviour or its gravity. This prohibition applies to any provider or deployer, public or private.

Yes, where the AI system is specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development and is not placed on the market or put into service in the Union. The Regulation does not apply to such systems under Article 2(6). Testing in real-world conditions is excluded from the scope only if it is conducted before the system is placed on the market or put into service, as provided by Article 2(8).

Yes, but the fine will be capped at the lower of the two amounts. For SMEs and start-ups, Article 99(6) sets the maximum fine at whichever is lower: the percentage of worldwide turnover or the fixed monetary amount. Since the violation concerns a prohibited practice under Article 5, Article 99(3) applies, with a ceiling of EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, subject to the SME reduction under Article 99(6).

Providers of high-risk AI systems must ensure compliance with the requirements of Chapter III Section 2, indicate their identity on the system or its packaging, operate a quality management system in accordance with Article 17, keep the technical documentation required under Article 11, retain automatically generated logs to the extent under their control, undergo the relevant conformity assessment procedure, draw up an EU declaration of conformity, affix the CE marking, comply with registration obligations, take corrective actions if non-compliant, and demonstrate conformity to competent authorities upon request (Article 16). The quality management system must be documented and include a regulatory compliance strategy, design and development controls, data management procedures, the risk management system under Article 9, post-market monitoring, and incident reporting processes (Article 17). The provider must keep the technical documentation, quality management documentation, notified body decisions (where applicable), and the EU declaration of conformity for 10 years after the system is placed on the market and make them available to national competent authorities (Article 18). Logs automatically generated by the system must be retained for at least six months, unless otherwise required by Union or national law (Article 19).

Yes, where the cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs. A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities and thus be classified as having systemic risk under Article 51(2) when its cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 floating-point operations. This classification triggers additional obligations under Article 55, including model evaluation with adversarial testing, systemic risk assessment and mitigation, serious incident reporting to the AI Office, and enhanced cybersecurity for the model and its infrastructure. The provider must continue to meet the baseline Article 53 obligations, which include maintaining technical documentation per Annex XI, supplying downstream providers with integration information per Annex XII, implementing a copyright compliance policy, and publishing a detailed training-data summary.

Training, validation and testing data sets for high-risk AI systems must be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose (Article 10(3)). They must be subject to data governance and management practices appropriate for the intended purpose, including examination for possible biases that could affect health and safety or fundamental rights (Article 10(2) and Article 10(2)(f)). Where strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, providers may process special categories of personal data under specific safeguards (Article 10(5)). These requirements apply only to testing data sets for high-risk AI systems not based on training AI models (Article 10(6)).

Article 99 sets out the administrative fines for non-compliance. Non-compliance with the prohibited practices in Article 5 is subject to fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or 7 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). Non-compliance with specified operator or notified-body obligations, including those under Articles 16, 22, 23, 24, 26, 31, 33(1), (3), (4), 34 and 50, is subject to fines of up to EUR 15 000 000 or 3 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher (Article 99(4)). Supplying incorrect, incomplete or misleading information to authorities is subject to fines of up to EUR 7 500 000 or 1 % of total worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher, with reduced ceilings for SMEs and start-ups under Article 99(6).

This question is about the NIS2 Directive (or the Cyber Resilience Act for product-level cyber requirements), not the EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689). This assistant only covers EU AI Act questions; consult the NIS2 Directive (or the Cyber Resilience Act for product-level cyber requirements) for the applicable rules.

Article 50(1) requires providers to design AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons so they are informed they are interacting with AI, unless this is obvious. Article 50(2) requires providers of generative AI to mark synthetic audio, image, video, or text in a machine-readable, detectable format. Article 50(3) requires deployers of emotion recognition or biometric categorisation systems to inform exposed natural persons of their operation.

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must use the system in accordance with the instructions for use (Article 26(1)), assign human oversight to competent natural persons (Article 26(2)), and monitor the system’s operation, informing the provider and relevant authorities of serious incidents or risks (Article 26(5)). They must keep automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months (Article 26(6)), and public authorities or Union bodies deploying such systems must ensure the system is registered in the EU database before use (Article 26(8)). Deployers who are employers must inform workers’ representatives and affected workers before deploying the system in the workplace (Article 26(7)), and deployers of systems listed in Annex III that make or assist in decisions affecting natural persons must inform those persons of the system’s use (Article 26(11)). Deployers that are financial institutions subject to Union financial services governance rules are deemed to fulfil the monitoring and log-keeping obligations by complying with those rules (Article 26(5) and (6), second subparagraphs).

Testing data is defined in Article 3(32) as data used to provide an independent evaluation of the AI system, in order to confirm its expected performance before it is placed on the market or put into service. It must be kept separate from the training and validation data so that this evaluation is genuinely independent. If testing data leaks into the training process, the system is in effect assessed on data it has already seen, which inflates its apparent performance and defeats the purpose of the independent check that Article 10 requires for the datasets of a high-risk AI system.

High-risk where the AI system is a safety component of a CE-marked medical device that is subject to third-party conformity assessment under Regulation (EU) 2017/745. The system is classified as high-risk under Article 6(1) because it concerns a product listed in Annex I and requires third-party conformity assessment. The conformity assessment follows the procedure of the applicable Union harmonisation legislation, with Chapter III Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment under Article 43(3).

The operator becomes a provider under Article 25(1)(c) by modifying the intended purpose to make the AI system high-risk, and must now fulfil all provider obligations under Article 16. These include ensuring compliance with the high-risk requirements of Chapter III, Section 2, undergoing conformity assessment under Article 43, drawing up technical documentation under Article 11, and registering the system under Article 49(1). The operator must also cooperate with the initial provider, who must provide necessary information and technical access under Article 25(2). If the operator's fine-tuning involved a general-purpose AI model and exceeded one-third of the base model’s compute, the Commission’s 18 July 2025 GPAI Guidelines clarify that the operator is a new provider, triggering additional obligations under Article 53.

Prohibited. The untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage to create or expand a facial recognition database is a prohibited practice under Article 5(1)(e). This prohibition applies to the placing on the market, putting into service, or use of such AI systems, regardless of the operator's status or sector.

Prohibited. An AI system that detects students' emotions via webcam constitutes an emotion recognition system under Article 3(39), and its use in an educational institution is prohibited under Article 5(1)(f), regardless of the vendor's characterisation as 'adaptive learning'. The prohibition applies unless the system is placed on the market strictly for medical or safety reasons, which is not indicated here.

A non-EU company placing a high-risk AI system on the EU market must appoint an authorised representative established in the Union by written mandate (Article 22). The authorised representative verifies that the EU declaration of conformity and technical documentation have been drawn up, keeps them available for authorities, and may be addressed by competent authorities on compliance matters (Article 22). The provider remains liable for all obligations, including conformity assessment, risk management, and post-market monitoring (Articles 43, 9, 72). Distributors in the EU must verify CE marking, documentation, and compliance before making the system available (Article 24).
